If anyone hasn't done something like this, it is easy to do. Likely for other DA/SA pistols as well.

 

You need a lubricating oil (just about anything will do), magnification, sharpie, 500 grit grit sand paper, toothpick, and maybe a metal section from a windshield wiper blade (or any other small flat metal support). You could repeat the process with 1000 grit and then lapping compound if you want mirror polish--- though I'm not sure it is worth the time for less than a match weapon and at that point don't fucking listen to me. Also you don't want to remove too much material. It depends on the weapon.

 

Find the sear and hammer interaction. Inspect with magnification. If you have not spent a lot of money on your platform the contact surfaces have defects/pitting/etc. You want to clean these mating surfaces so the hammer 'cleanly' releases from the sear. Depending on how the surface quality is you can use two techniques. The first is for only 'small' imperfections. 1) cut a small strip of 500 grit that fits and fills the contact between the sear and hammer. Pull back the hammer and place the paper between the hammer/sear contact area. Only use a single thickness. Lower the hammer so the sandpaper is clamped between it and the sear. Hold down sear and pull paper out. Repeat around a dozen times. Inspect. If no progress is being made then try 2). If progress is made flip paper and clean the hammer side in the same manner. If not use technique 2) described below with the following. You can use the sharpie to ink the sear/hammer. Then lower the hammer onto the sear and pull the trigger. Look for the removal/transfer of the ink between the surfaces. The contact points should have removed ink and be 'shiny'. The end goal is even contact along the sear/hammer interaction. You may find the hammer and sear have different hardness so you could favor the side you tune for ease. You may have to do this a few times and using fresh pieces of sandpaper. Once the surface starts looking better stop swapping the paper so frequently and use a drop of oil for a wet polish. This will go slower but provide a finer finish. 2) If your material is hard enough (as in the case of the CZ I most recently worked on) the dry 500 grit wrapped around a toothpick/metal will work much better. Be sure and match the angle of the sear and hammer. This technique allows a little more force on the polish for better progress.
